questions.stem: In a rural ED you are examining Marge, 28, who has crampy right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and jaundice. You tell the examiner you will now test for Murphy's sign. How do you elicit it?
options: Press deeply in the right upper quadrant, release quickly and watch for pain on release
Press in the left iliac fossa and watch for pain felt in the right upper quadrant
Rest fingers under the right costal margin, then ask her to take a deep breath in
Strike a fist placed over the right lower ribs and watch for a wince of pain
questions.why: Place your fingers below the right costal margin at the midclavicular line and ask her to breathe in deeply. The sign is positive if she stops breathing in because the inflamed gallbladder hits your hand, and the same manoeuvre on the left side does not hurt.
notes: This tests rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not specific to the gallbladder and is unkind to a patient already in severe pain.
This is Rovsing's sign, used for appendicitis, and she has already had her appendix out.
This is percussion tenderness over the liver (or a renal punch if done at the loin). It does not test whether the gallbladder catches on inspiration.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has acute cholangitis from a distal common bile duct stone in a rural ED: T 39.1 °C, HR 124, SBP 98, lactate 2.6, creatinine normal, no drug allergies (shellfish only). Blood cultures have just been taken. Per eTG, which empirical antibiotic regimen should be started now?
options: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 4-hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly
Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally 12-hourly, review in 24 hours
questions.why: eTG first line for biliary sepsis is amoxicillin (covers enterococci) plus gentamicin (covers gram-negative enteric bacilli such as E. coli and Klebsiella). Give it within 60 minutes, then set the gentamicin interval by renal function.
notes: This regimen has no reliable cover for the gram-negative enteric bacilli that cause most cholangitis. Anaerobic cover is not routinely needed unless she has had a biliary-enteric anastomosis.
Flucloxacillin targets staphylococci and does not cover enterococci, a key biliary pathogen. It is the wrong beta-lactam for this infection.
She is septic with rigors, tachycardia and a falling blood pressure, so she needs IV antibiotics now. Oral therapy is only for step-down once she has improved.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has a 9 mm stone obstructing the distal common bile duct. For two days her stools have been pale and her urine dark. Her bilirubin is 68 µmol/L, of which 54 is conjugated, with ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases. What best explains her dark urine?
options: Retained bile salts spill into the blood and are excreted in the urine
Unconjugated bilirubin from red cell breakdown is filtered by the kidneys
Extra urobilinogen reabsorbed from the gut is excreted by the kidneys
Conjugated bilirubin refluxes into the blood and, being water-soluble, is filtered
questions.why: In post-hepatic obstruction, conjugated (glucuronidated, water-soluble) bilirubin backs up into the blood and is filtered at the glomerulus, which darkens the urine. Bile cannot reach the gut, so no stercobilin forms and the stools are pale.
notes: Retained bile salts cause her itch, but they do not colour the urine.
Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not filtered, so pre-hepatic jaundice gives normal-coloured urine. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated.
Urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin that reaches the bowel. A blocked duct reduces urobilinogen, it does not increase it.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has a 9 mm stone in the distal common bile duct and is transferred for ERCP. The endoscopist passes a side-viewing duodenoscope to cannulate the bile duct at its opening and perform a sphincterotomy. Where does the common bile duct open into the gut?
options: Major duodenal papilla, posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum
Minor duodenal papilla, proximal to the major papilla in the second part
Posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, just distal to the pylorus
Medial wall of the third part, behind the superior mesenteric vessels
questions.why: The common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater). This opens through the sphincter of Oddi at the major duodenal papilla, about halfway down the descending (second) part of the duodenum. That is why a stone here can also cause gallstone pancreatitis.
notes: The minor papilla drains the accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), not the bile duct. Cannulating it would not reach the stone.
The common bile duct runs behind the first part of the duodenum but does not open there. It continues behind the pancreatic head to the second part.
The third part crosses behind the superior mesenteric vessels and receives no duct. Duodenal compression here is the SMA syndrome.
